items.title: reduce without a start value throws on empty arrays
items.body:
Without a starting value, `reduce` uses the first element as the accumulator and starts at the second. For a non-empty list of prices that still gives the right total, which is why the tests pass. But when nothing is in stock, `filter` returns an empty array, `map` keeps it empty, and `reduce` has nothing to start from: it **throws a TypeError**. The lesson's rule: always give `reduce` a starting value.

Why the others are wrong:
- **undefined, renders blank**: an empty array without a start value throws; it does not return `undefined`.
- **defaults the accumulator to 0**: `reduce` never guesses a default.
- **skips the first price**: the first price becomes the starting accumulator, so it is still included.

excerpts.quote: .map(p => p.price) .reduce((sum, price) => sum + price, 0);
Always give `reduce` a starting value (the `0`); without it, `reduce` on an empty array throws a `TypeError`.

items.title: Spread copies only the outer object
items.body:
`{ ...profile }` creates a new outer object, but each property value is copied as-is. `address` is itself an object, so the draft gets a reference to the **same** address object the profile holds. Changing `draft.address.city` changes that shared object, so the profile shows the new city even after Cancel. Lesson 01 shows this exact effect, and `structuredClone` as the way to copy nested data.

Why the others are wrong:
- **const forwards writes**: `const` has nothing to do with it; the objects are shared.
- **Cancel merges back**: nothing merges; the original was changed directly.
- **spread copies nested objects with linked getters**: spread does not copy nested objects at all.

excerpts.quote: const shallow = { ...original }; shallow.name = "Riley"; shallow.address.city = "Denver"; console.log(original.name, original.address.city); // Sam Denver
But `address` is itself an object, and only its reference was copied, so changing `shallow.address.city` also changed `original.address.city`.

items.title: var gives every closure the same i
items.body:
A `var` declared in a `for` loop belongs to the whole function, so there is only **one** `i`. Each arrow function closes over that same variable, not a copy of its value at the time. By the time any handler runs, the loop has finished and `i` is 3, so all of them report 3. With `let`, the loop creates a **new binding for each iteration**, so each closure keeps its own value: 0, 1, 2. The lesson shows both versions side by side.

Why the others are wrong:
- **a global shared by all scripts**: inside a function, `var` is function-scoped; renaming does not change the sharing.
- **arrows copy at call time; use function**: a regular function closes over the same single `i`; only `let` fixes it.
- **captured by value, move push**: closures capture variables, not values.

excerpts.quote: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { fnsVar.push(() => i); } console.log(fnsVar.map(f => f())); // [ 3, 3, 3 ]
With `var`, there is one `i` for the whole function, and every closure sees its final value, `3`. With `let`, each loop iteration gets its own `j`.

items.title: Number of an empty string is 0
items.body:
`Number("")` is **0**, not `NaN`. So a blank field converts to 0, `Number.isNaN(0)` is false, the validator lets it through, and the order goes in for 0 items. The lesson calls this a common source of "empty field counted as zero" bugs. A correct validator checks for blank input separately (and here, for a quantity of at least 1).

Why the others are wrong:
- **blanks arrive as null**: form fields give strings; a blank one is `""`.
- **Number.isNaN coerces**: `Number.isNaN` does not coerce; the coercion happened in `Number("")`.
- **Number("") throws**: it returns 0 without throwing.

excerpts.quote: console.log(Number(""), Number("  42 "), Number("abc")); // 0 42 NaN
Note that `Number("")` is `0`, not `NaN`, which is a common source of "empty field counted as zero" bugs.

items.title: await pauses only its own function
items.body:
Inside `loadPosts`, `await fetch(...)` pauses `loadPosts` until the response arrives. It does **not** pause the code that called `loadPosts`. The caller receives a promise and continues straight to the next line, which reads the list before the request has finished, so it is still empty. To wait, the caller must `await loadPosts()` too (or use `.then`).

Why the others are wrong:
- **async functions return undefined**: they return a promise, which can be awaited.
- **a stale cached response**: no caching is involved; the request simply has not finished.
- **await blocks the whole program**: the lesson says the opposite.

excerpts.quote: `await` pauses only inside the current async function, not the entire program.
Instead of blocking everything, JavaScript schedules follow-up work. Promises represent values that may be available later.

items.title: Concept: values, references and side effects
items.body:
Two ideas from the lessons explain a surprising number of bugs.

**Objects are shared by reference.** A variable holding an object holds a pointer to it. Assigning the variable elsewhere, or copying only the outer layer, leaves both sides pointing at the same inner objects. Lesson 01 shows when a copy is really independent and when it is not.

**Pure functions versus side effects.** Lesson 02 defines a pure function as one whose output depends only on its inputs and which changes nothing outside itself. A side effect is any other change the caller can observe: mutating an argument or shared object, writing to the screen, saving, sending a request. Side effects are what apps are for; the skill is keeping them in a few obvious places.

When you read a snippet, ask: which objects are shared, and which lines change something outside the function?

excerpts.quote: ### Making a real copy If you need an independent object, create one:
A function is **pure** when its output depends only on its inputs and it changes nothing outside itself.
Side effects are not bad. Apps exist to cause them.

items.title: Concept: the five-step bug routine
items.body:
Lesson 01 ends with a debugging walkthrough and says to use the same order for every bug in the course:

1. **Reproduce it**, in the smallest code you can.
2. **State the expected behaviour** in one sentence.
3. **Inspect the actual values and their types.** Log them; do not guess. `typeof` is your friend.
4. **Fix the cause, not the symptom.** Find where the bad value entered and correct it there.
5. **Re-test the failure path too**, not just the happy path.

Step 3 matters most in JavaScript, because so many bugs in these lessons come from a value being a different type than you assumed: a string from a form, `null` from an API, an object where you expected a copy. Most quiz questions describe a symptom; run this routine on each one before you look at the choices.

excerpts.quote: 1. **Reproduce it.** Run the snippet. It prints `105`, so the bug is real and small enough to study. 2. **State the expected behaviour in one sentence.** "10 plus 5 should be 15." 3. **Inspect the actual values and their types.** Do not guess; log them.

items.title: Braces mean you must write return
items.body:
`p => p * 1.1` has a single expression after the arrow, and an arrow function returns that expression automatically. `p => { p * 1.1 }` has braces, which make a **function body**. A body runs its statements and returns `undefined` unless it says `return`. So every call returns `undefined` and `map` builds an array of `undefined`. The fix is `p => { console.log(p); return p * 1.1; }`.

Why the others are wrong:
- **map skips block-scoped callbacks**: `map` calls every callback and stores whatever it returns.
- **returns an object literal**: braces after `=>` are a body, not an object; you would need parentheses for an object.
- **runs asynchronously**: function bodies run synchronously.

excerpts.quote: An arrow function with a single expression after `=>` returns that expression automatically. As soon as you add `{ }`, you must write `return`.
const doubleBlockBroken = (n) => { n * 2; }; console.log(doubleBroken(4), doubleBlockBroken(4)); // undefined undefined

items.title: Convert before the arithmetic, not after
items.body:
Form values are strings. `"10" + 5` is string concatenation, which gives `"105"`. Wrapping the result in `Number(...)` turns `"105"` into the number **105**, which is still wrong. The damage was done when `+` joined the strings. The fix has to happen where the string enters the code: convert the input with `Number(quantityInput)`, check it with `Number.isNaN`, and only then add. The lesson calls the wrapping a tempting wrong fix.

Why the others are wrong:
- **works but parseInt is faster**: it does not work; speed is irrelevant.
- **breaks decimals by rounding**: `Number` does not round; and the result is wrong even for integers.
- **NaN for any concatenated string**: `Number("105")` is a perfectly valid 105.

excerpts.quote: const totalItems = quantityInput + extraItems; console.log(totalItems); // 105
The tempting wrong fix is `totalItems - 0` or wrapping the final result in `Number(...)`. `Number("105")` is `105`, which is still wrong. The data was already damaged when the strings were joined

items.title: Defaults apply only to undefined
items.body:
A default parameter like `name = "friend"` is used only when the argument is `undefined`, either missing or passed as `undefined`. `null` is a real value, so `greet(null)` uses it and prints "Hi, null". The lesson's example shows all four cases. The fix is to turn `null` into `undefined` (or use `??`) where the API data enters your code.

Why the others are wrong:
- **any explicit value, even undefined, skips it**: explicitly passing `undefined` does trigger the default.
- **every falsy value except null**: only `undefined` triggers it; `0` or `""` would be used as-is.
- **evaluated once and overwritten**: defaults are evaluated on each call that needs them.

excerpts.quote: console.log(greet(), greet(undefined), greet(null), greet("Sam")); // Hi, friend Hi, friend Hi, null Hi, Sam
A default parameter is used only when the argument is `undefined` (missing or passed explicitly). `null` is a real value, so `greet(null)` prints `Hi, null`.

items.title: Each factory call gets its own count
items.body:
Every call to `makeCounter()` runs `let count = 0` again, creating a **new**, private `count` for the function it returns. `counter` has its own `count`, already at 2; `other` has a brand-new one at 0. So `other()` prints 1 and `counter()` prints 3: "1 3". The lesson shows this exact line and sums it up as two closures, two private variables.

Why the others are wrong:
- **3 4, one shared count**: the variable is declared inside the factory, so each call makes its own.
- **undefined 3**: closures keep access to `count` after `makeCounter` returns; that is what a closure is.
- **1 1, reset**: creating `other` does not touch `counter`'s variable.

excerpts.quote: const other = makeCounter(); console.log(other(), counter()); // 1 3
`other` starts at 1 because it has its own `count`. `counter` continues from 2 to 3. Two closures, two private variables.

items.title: Hidden shared state makes results depend on history
items.body:
`addToCartTotal` adds to `cart.total`, an object shared by everything that imports it. Its result depends on what earlier calls already did: if another test added 10 first, the total is now 20, and the assertion of 10 fails. `withItemAdded(total, amount)` is pure: it reads only its inputs and changes nothing, so the same inputs always give the same output, no matter what ran before. That is what makes it easy to test.

Why the others are wrong:
- **only because a parameter lets tests pass the cart**: the point is that it reads and changes nothing outside itself.
- **shared objects reset between tests**: they do not; that is exactly why the order matters.
- **writing to an object is slower**: speed is not the issue; correctness is.

excerpts.quote: function addToCartTotal(amount) { cart.total += amount;            // side effect: changes shared state
Calling `addToCartTotal(10)` twice gives a different result each time because it depends on hidden state. Calling `withItemAdded(0, 10)` twice gives `10` both times.

items.title: const fixes the name, not the object
items.body:
`const DEFAULTS = {...}` means the name `DEFAULTS` can never be pointed at a different object. It says nothing about the object itself, so `DEFAULTS.theme = "dark"` is allowed and changes the one shared object that every page uses. The lesson shows exactly this: changing a property of a `const` object works, while reassigning the `const` name throws. To protect the object you need something else, such as `Object.freeze` or working on copies.

Why the others are wrong:
- **protects everything except strings**: `const` protects no properties at all.
- **freezes only in strict mode**: `const` never freezes objects, in any mode.
- **created a new shadowing DEFAULTS**: a property assignment changes the existing object; it creates no new variable.

excerpts.quote: const settings = { theme: "light" }; settings.theme = "dark"; console.log(settings.theme); // dark
`const` means the **label** cannot be pointed somewhere else. It says nothing about whether the object it points to can change.

items.title: An empty array is truthy
items.body:
In an `if`, every value counts as true or false. The falsy values are `0`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN` and `false`, and nothing else. An empty array is an object, and every object is truthy, so `if (results)` passes even when `results` is `[]`. The page renders an empty list instead of "No matches". The lesson's fix: write `results.length > 0` when you mean "if there are items".

Why the others are wrong:
- **arrays coerce to their first element**: `if` does not look inside the array.
- **the check ran before the fetch**: the symptom happens with the real `[]`.
- **only checks it was declared**: `if` tests the value; an undeclared name would throw, not pass.

excerpts.quote: // false for: 0, "", null, undefined, NaN, false // true for:  "0", " ", [], {}, -1   (and every other value)
Empty arrays and empty objects are truthy, which surprises people who expect `if (items)` to mean "if there are items". Use `items.length > 0` for that.

items.title: Start here: lessons 01 and 02, run every snippet
items.body:
trainjs is a JavaScript course in `docs/lessons/`, ten lessons from foundations to React, plus advanced, capstone and interview material. This pack draws almost entirely on the first two lessons, with one question from lesson 05:

1. `docs/lessons/01-javascript-foundations.md`: values and types, copies, `const`, equality, coercion, truthy and falsy, and a debugging walkthrough.
2. `docs/lessons/02-functions-scope-data.md`: pure functions, the three ways to write a function, scope and closures, arrays and `reduce`, default parameters.
3. `docs/lessons/05-async-fetch-apis.md`: the concepts section on `await`.

The lessons put each snippet's output in a comment at the end of the line (`// Sam Denver`). Before reading that comment, cover it and predict the output yourself; then run the snippet in Node or the browser console to check. Most questions in this pack are exactly that kind of prediction, applied to a realistic bug.

excerpts.quote: ## Goals - Use conditionals and loops without losing readability. - Understand function inputs, outputs, and side effects. - Learn scope and closures well enough to explain them.
Work through it in the same order you will use for every bug in this course.
